subtype: Real hurt versus a habitual role [Observer]
passage:
Supervisor's note, Thursday. Sudha, customer support floor.
Two complaints reached me this week, and I nearly handled them the wrong way round.
Ritesh came in calm, as he does most weeks. His story: the night team dumps tickets on him, nobody values him, he is always left out. It is the fifth such story since January. Each has a different villain and the same sufferer.
Pankaj came in red-faced, almost shouting that his overtime hours had been logged under someone else's name. I nearly told him to come back when he could speak calmly.
I checked the logs before responding. Pankaj was right: his hours had been moved. He had been wronged, and he was simply upset about it.
Next steps: corrected Pankaj's hours and apologised to him. Booked a separate talk with Ritesh to ask what change he actually wants.

qa.q: What did Pankaj say had happened to his overtime hours?
qa.a: Pankaj said his overtime hours had been logged under someone else's name.

qa.q: Why did Sudha nearly tell Pankaj to come back later?
qa.a: Sudha was put off by the shouting and half assumed an upset person must be less reliable, which almost led to judging him wrongly.

qa.q: Which choice by Sudha turned the week around?
qa.a: Checking the logs before responding showed Pankaj had truly been wronged; correcting the hours and booking a separate talk with Ritesh treated each case on its facts.

qa.q: How might Pankaj have felt if Sudha had sent him away for being upset?
qa.a: He would have felt wronged twice, first by the moved hours and then by not being believed because he was angry.

grounding: A supervisor notices the difference between Ritesh's repeated stories of always being the sufferer and Pankaj's real, angry complaint, and checks the facts before judging.

subtype: Real hurt versus a habitual role [Observer]
passage:
Tuesday night
Simran cried in the office corridor today, and my first thought was: here we go again.
I know that's unkind. But in eight months of sitting next to her, every week has had a new villain. The printer technician was out to get her. The manager hates her. The canteen staff did it on purpose. I've started nodding without listening.
Today she said Harsh presented her budget sheet as his own in the client meeting. I nearly said "hmm" and walked on. Then I remembered watching her build that sheet, formula by formula, last Thursday.
So I said, "I saw you make it. Do you want me to tell the manager that?" She stopped crying and stared, like she didn't expect anyone to believe her.
Note to self: the pattern is real. So was this. Check before deciding.
Vijay

qa.q: What did Harsh present as his own?
qa.a: Harsh presented Simran's budget sheet as his own in the client meeting.

qa.q: Why was Vijay's first thought "here we go again"?
qa.a: Vijay felt tired of Simran's weekly stories with new villains and had stopped really listening, so the tears seemed like more of the same.

qa.q: What small step made Vijay's response fair?
qa.a: Vijay remembered watching Simran build the sheet and offered to tell the manager, checking the facts instead of judging by the old pattern.

qa.q: What might it have meant to Simran that Vijay believed her?
qa.a: She seemed surprised, as if she didn't expect to be believed, so it may have felt like relief at being taken seriously for once.

grounding: Vijay, who sits beside Simran and is tired of her weekly stories of villains, nearly dismisses a real grievance, then checks what was seen and backs her.
